What the law should mandate is the burden of proof be with the officer, to prove any claims by citizens, to be falsified using the police's video - as opposed to the other way around. No video - the police is guilty. No video - the incident did not happen. No video - the claimant's claim is factual.

This is not a case where there was justification for the camera to be shut down; however, I think society should recognize circumstances/privacy concerns exist that justify the ability to shut down a camera. Most commonly the arguments I've heard and agree with are "What about an officer who needs to relieve him/herself while on duty? What about an officer who is taking a report from a victim of sexual assault? Or is present on a medical call where HIPAA information is being provided?" It's my understanding that such footage is generally defaulted to public record in many municipalities assuming its not evidence of an active criminal investigation, and can thus can eventually be requested for release by a member of the public (the same way an employer might run your record during a criminal background check).

My point in saying all this is, I don't think designing recording devices that cannot be shut down at officers' discretion is necessarily the solution, as I think there exist times where they shouldn't be recording, but I think changing the way such an action is taken might solve the problem.

At an old job of mine we had "tokens" that were the size of a car key fob that produced a random number sequence that reset every minute, and this was required to sign into your computer. Locking your computer could be done in literally less than a second, but signing in was a more tedious process due to the use of the token. I think bodycams should operate similarly, where turning them on can be done in a snap, but powering them down requires a tedious process that can't be done without focused intent. In addition to preserving the ability of officers to shut down the cameras in the cases described above, I think this solves the issues we worry about as citizens with a reasonable fear of law enforcement abuses:

  • It makes it so shutting down the camera is, for all intents and purposes, impossible in the midst of a truly high-stress situation, and these are really what we're trying to see with these cameras in the first place. Cases where the officer was truly "in fear of his her or life" and possessing the cognitive ability and fine motor skills to type a random number sequence to shut off the camera would be incongruent.

  • Turning off the camera becomes understood as deliberate and intentional, and not something the officer could have done "accidentally" in the midst of performing his/her duties, requiring forethought and justification to perform the action.
